questions.problem:
Consider the d’Alembert differential equation

$$
y=x{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}).
$$

If ${y}^{′}(x)=t,$ then general solution can be expressed in parametric form $(x(t),y(t)),$ where

$$
y(t)=(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-t+C}{(1-t)^{2}})f(t)+g(t)
$$

and $C$ is an arbitrary constant. Find $f(t)+g(t).$

*Hint: Under the given transformation, we have*

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{2x}{t-1}=\frac{1}{t(1-t)}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A differential equation is a d'Alembert differential equation if it can be expressed in the form

$$
y=xf({y}^{′})+g({y}^{′}),
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are differentiable functions of ${y}^{′}.$ 

We're told that, under the substitution ${y}^{′}(x)=t,$ our d’Alembert differential equation transforms to the first-order linear equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{2x}{t-1}=\frac{1}{t(1-t)}
$$

We'll solve this equation using the method of integrating factors. Since this equation is already of the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t)
$$

we compute our integrating factor as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int P(t)\,\text{d}t} \\  & ={e}^{\int 2/(t-1)\,\text{d}t} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|t-1|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(t-1)^{2}} \\  & =(t-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying our differential equation by $I(t)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(t-1)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(t-1)^{2}\frac{2x}{t-1}=(t-1)^{2}\frac{1}{t(1-t)} \\ (t-1)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2(t-1)x=-(t-1)^{2}\frac{1}{t(t-1)} \\ (t-1)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2(t-1)x=-\frac{t-1}{t} \\ (t-1)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2(t-1)x=\frac{1-t}{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Rewriting the left-hand side as an exact derivative, and integrating both sides of the equation with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x(t-1)^{2}) & =\frac{1-t}{t} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x(t-1)^{2})\,\text{d}t & =\int \frac{1-t}{t}\,\text{d}t \\ x(t-1)^{2} & =\int \frac{1}{t}-1\,\text{d}t \\ x(t-1)^{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-t+C \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-t+C}{(t-1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
x(t)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-t+C}{(t-1)^{2}}.
$$

To recover $y$, we substitute $x$ into

$$
y=x{t}^{2}+t,
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-t+C}{(t-1)^{2}}){t}^{2}+t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $f(t)={t}^{2},g(t)=t,$ and

$$
f(t)+g(t)={t}^{2}+t.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the d’Alembert differential equation

$$
y=x(3+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})+2{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}.
$$

If ${y}^{′}(x)=t,$ then general solution can be expressed in parametric form $(x(t),y(t)),$ where

$$
x(t)=C{e}^{-t/3}+f(t)
$$

and $C$ is an arbitrary constant. Find the function $f(t).$

*Hint: Under the given transformation, we have*

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{3}x=-\frac{4}{3}t.
$$

*You may also wish to make use of the following result (constants omitted):*

$$
\int t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t=(t-1){e}^{t}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A differential equation is a d'Alembert differential equation if it can be expressed in the form

$$
y=xf({y}^{′})+g({y}^{′}),
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are differentiable functions of ${y}^{′}.$ 

We're told that, under the substitution ${y}^{′}(x)=t,$ our d’Alembert differential equation transforms to the first-order linear equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{3}x=-\frac{4}{3}t.
$$

We'll solve this equation using the method of integrating factors. Since this equation is already of the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t),
$$

we compute our integrating factor as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int P(t)\,\text{d}t}={e}^{\int \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}t}={e}^{t/3}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying our differential equation by $I(t)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{t/3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{3}x{e}^{t/3} & =-\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{t/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Rewriting the left-hand side as an exact derivative, and integrating both sides of the equation with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x{e}^{t/3}) & =-\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{t/3} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x{e}^{t/3})\,\text{d}t & =-\frac{4}{3}\int t{e}^{t/3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the integral, let $u=\frac{t}{3}.$ Then $t=3u$ and $\text{d}t=3\,\text{d}u,$ so

$$
\begin{aligned}\int t{e}^{t/3}\,\text{d}t & =\int (3u){e}^{u}\cdot 3\,\text{d}u \\  & =9\int u{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =9(u-1){e}^{u}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting back $u=\frac{t}{3},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int t{e}^{t/3}\,\text{d}t & =9(\frac{t}{3}-1){e}^{t/3} \\  & =(3t-9){e}^{t/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}x{e}^{t/3} & =-\frac{4}{3}(3t-9){e}^{t/3}+C \\  & =(-4t+12){e}^{t/3}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
x=-4t+12+C{e}^{-t/3}.
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
x(t)=C{e}^{-t/3}+12-4t
$$

and finally, $f(t)=12-4t.$

questions.problem:
Consider the d’Alembert differential equation

$$
y=x(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3)+2{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}.
$$

If ${y}^{′}(x)=t,$ then general solution can be expressed in parametric form $(x(t),y(t)),$ where

$$
y(t)=(C{e}^{t/3}-4t-12)f(t)+g(t)
$$

and $C$ is an arbitrary constant. Find $f(t)+g(t).$

*Hint: Under the given transformation, we have*

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\frac{1}{3}x=\frac{4}{3}t.
$$

*You may also wish to make use of the following result (constants omitted):*

$$
\int t{e}^{-t/3}\,\text{d}t=(-3t-9){e}^{-t/3}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A differential equation is a d'Alembert differential equation if it can be expressed in the form

$$
y=xf({y}^{′})+g({y}^{′}),
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are differentiable functions of ${y}^{′}.$ 

We're told that, under the substitution ${y}^{′}(x)=t,$ our d’Alembert differential equation transforms to the first-order linear equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\frac{1}{3}x=\frac{4}{3}t.
$$

We'll solve this equation using the method of integrating factors. Since this equation is already of the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t)
$$

we compute our integrating factor as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int P(t)\,\text{d}t} \\  & ={e}^{\int (-\frac{1}{3})\,\text{d}t} \\  & ={e}^{-t/3}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying our differential equation by $I(t)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t/3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\frac{1}{3}x{e}^{-t/3} & =\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{-t/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Rewriting the left-hand side as an exact derivative, and integrating both sides of the equation with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x{e}^{-t/3}) & =\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{-t/3} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x{e}^{-t/3})\,\text{d}t & =\frac{4}{3}\int t{e}^{-t/3}\,\text{d}t \\ x{e}^{-t/3} & =\frac{4}{3}(-3t-9){e}^{-t/3}+C \\ x & =-4t-12+C{e}^{t/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
x(t)=C{e}^{t/3}-4t-12.
$$

To recover $y$, we substitute $x$ into

$$
y=x(t-3)+2{t}^{2},
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =(C{e}^{t/3}-4t-12)(t-3)+2{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $f(t)=t-3,\text{ }g(t)=2{t}^{2},$ and

$$
f(t)+g(t)=2{t}^{2}+t-3.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the d’Alembert differential equation, defined for $t>0:$

$$
y=x{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

Using the substitution $t=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ the equation can be transformed to a first-order linear equation of the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t).
$$

Find the functions $P$ and $Q.$

$\,\,P(t)=$
{{field-1}}$,\,Q(t)=$
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
A differential equation is a d'Alembert differential equation if it can be expressed in the form

$$
y=xf({y}^{′})+g({y}^{′}),
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are differentiable functions of ${y}^{′}.$ 

In our case, we wish to transform the equation

$$
y=x{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

into a first-order linear equation for $x=x(t).$ We proceed in three steps:

**Step 1**: Substitute, and differentiate with respect to $x.$

We have the substitution

$$
t=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Substituting this into the equation gives

$$
y=x{t}^{2}+3t.
$$

Differentiating both sides with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x{t}^{2}+3t).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the sum and product rules and using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x{t}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3t) \\ t & ={t}^{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)+x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({t}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3t) \\ t & ={t}^{2}+2xt\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}+3\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Isolate the derivative and take its reciprocal.

We isolate $\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}t-{t}^{2} & =2xt\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}+3\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x} \\ t(1-t) & =(2xt+3)\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x} \\ \frac{t(1-t)}{2xt+3} & =\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{t(1-t)}{2xt+3}.
$$

Therefore, by taking the reciprocal of each side, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2xt+3}{t(1-t)}.
$$

**Step 3**: Express the derivative as a first-order linear equation.

Finally, we write this in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t)
$$

as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{2xt+3}{t(1-t)} \\ t(1-t)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2xt+3 \\ t(1-t)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-2xt & =3 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\frac{2xt}{t(1-t)} & =\frac{3}{t(1-t)} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\frac{2x}{1-t} & =\frac{3}{t(1-t)} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{2x}{t-1} & =\frac{3}{t(1-t)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(t)=\frac{2}{t-1},\,Q(t)=\frac{3}{t(1-t)}.
$$

Consider the d’Alembert differential equation

$$
y=xcos\,(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})-3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Using the substitution $t=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ the equation can be transformed to a first-order linear equation of the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t).
$$

Find the functions $P$ and $Q.$

$\,\,P(t)=$
{{field-1}}$,\,Q(t)=$
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
A differential equation is a d'Alembert differential equation if it can be expressed in the form

$$
y=xf({y}^{′})+g({y}^{′}),
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are differentiable functions of ${y}^{′}.$ 

In our case, we wish to transform the equation

$$
y=xcos\,(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})-3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

into a first-order linear equation for $x=x(t).$ We proceed in three steps:

**Step 1**: Substitute, and differentiate with respect to $x.$

We have the substitution

$$
t=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Substituting this into the equation gives

$$
y=x\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-3t.
$$

Differentiating both sides with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-3t).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the sum and product rules and using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3t) \\ t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)+x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3t) \\ t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}-3\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Isolate the derivative and take its reciprocal.

We isolate $\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}t-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & =-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}-3\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x} \\ t-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & =-(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+3)\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x} \\ -\frac{t-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)}{x\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+3} & =\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t}{x\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+3}.
$$

Therefore, by taking the reciprocal of each side, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{x\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+3}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t}.
$$

**Step 3**: Express the derivative as a first-order linear equation.

Finally, we write this in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t)
$$

as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{x\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+3}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t} \\ (\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+3 \\ (\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =3 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\frac{x\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t} & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{x\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)}{t-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)} & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(t)=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)}{t-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)},\,Q(t)=\frac{3}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t}.
$$
